[PATH:empirical] Comparative empirical study of fixed-step vs. adaptive-step methods in non-stationary optimization benchmarks (e.g., moving peaks, rotating hyperplane problems) — Directly tests the hypothesis by measuring convergence quality and risk of suboptimality under controlled non-stationary conditions with limited budget.

[PATH:theoretical] Theoretical analysis of fixed-step gradient descent convergence bounds under time-varying objective functions (e.g., regret bounds or dynamic regret in online convex optimization) — Provides formal guarantees or counterexamples regarding how fixed step sizes affect convergence optimality when the problem changes, clarifying the mechanism behind the hypothesized risk.

[PATH:literature] Literature review on adaptive step-size strategies (e.g., AdaGrad, RMSProp, or line search) for non-stationary optimization, comparing their performance to fixed-step baselines — Synthesizes existing evidence on whether fixed-step methods indeed show higher suboptimal convergence rates in dynamic environments, supporting or refuting the hypothesis via accumulated empirical and theoretical findings.

qualifier.temporal: during periods of non-stationarity or rapid change in the problem space

C005.subject: Fixed-step methods

[PATH:empirical] Controlled benchmark experiments comparing fixed-step optimizers (e.g., SGD with fixed LR) against adaptive methods (e.g., Adam) across a suite of deep learning tasks with limited computational budgets, measuring the variance in performance across hyperparameter configurations. — Directly tests whether fixed-step methods require more tuning to achieve comparable results under budget constraints, providing concrete data to confirm or refute the hypothesis.

[PATH:theoretical] Theoretical analysis of convergence rates for fixed-step gradient-based methods under bounded gradient noise, deriving the sensitivity of convergence to step-size choices as a function of budget. — Provides formal bounds on how hyperparameter misspecification degrades performance, clarifying whether fixed-step methods inherently demand more tuning in resource-limited settings.

[PATH:literature] Systematic literature review of empirical studies (e.g., from NeurIPS, ICML, ICLR) that report hyperparameter tuning effort for fixed-step vs. adaptive methods in optimization with limited compute. — Aggregates existing evidence across many studies to assess whether there is a consensus that fixed-step methods increase tuning burden, addressing the disputed status of the hypothesis.

C006.subject: Adaptive algorithms with explicit change-point detection
C006.predicate: outperform both standard adaptive algorithms and fixed-step methods
C006.object: in non-stationary environments where the frequency of distribution shifts is unknown and variable
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: Adaptive algorithms with explicit change-point detection in non-stationary environments where the frequency of distribution shifts is unknown and variable]

[PATH:empirical] Comparative benchmark experiments on synthetic non-stationary datasets with varying shift frequencies (e.g., rotating hyperplane, abrupt vs. gradual drift) — Directly tests whether explicit change-point detectors (e.g., ADWIN, BOCD) yield lower cumulative regret or faster adaptation than fixed-step (e.g., constant learning rate SGD) and standard adaptive methods (e.g., AdaGrad, Adam) when shift intervals are unknown and variable.

[PATH:theoretical] Regret bounds analysis for algorithms with change-point detection under unknown, variable shift intervals (e.g., minimax lower bounds or dynamic regret analysis) — Deriving or extending theoretical guarantees (e.g., O(√T) regret with known change points vs. O(T^{2/3}) under unknown intervals) can confirm or refute the claimed superiority by quantifying the cost of detection delay and false alarms.

[PATH:literature] Meta-analysis of existing empirical studies comparing change-point detection-based learners (e.g., FHDDM, RDDM) against non-adaptive baselines in online learning benchmarks (e.g., MOA, scikit-multiflow) — Surveying published results across diverse drift scenarios (e.g., real-world data streams like electricity pricing, forest cover type) can reveal whether the advantage holds consistently or only under specific conditions, thus supporting or challenging the hypothesis.

C007.subject: Fixed-step methods
C007.object: in terms of simplicity and computational efficiency
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: Fixed-step methods in terms of simplicity and computational efficiency]

[PATH:empirical] Benchmark experiments comparing fixed-step gradient descent vs. Adam/Adagrad on non-stationary (e.g., noisy or drifting) and multi-modal functions (e.g., Rastrigin, Ackley) from the COCO (Comparing Continuous Optimizers) platform — Direct empirical comparison under the specified domain conditions can reveal whether fixed-step methods maintain competitive performance in simplicity and efficiency, especially when adaptive methods incur overhead from step-size tuning.

[PATH:theoretical] Theoretical analysis of convergence rates for fixed-step vs. adaptive methods in non-stationary convex optimization (e.g., using regret bounds or oracle complexity models) — A formal proof or counterexample showing that fixed-step methods achieve near-optimal regret in non-stationary settings (due to lower per-iteration cost) would support the hypothesis; otherwise, adaptive methods may be fundamentally necessary.

[PATH:literature] Historical review of optimization literature from the 1990s (e.g., papers on stochastic approximation, Kiefer-Wolfowitz, or early neural network training) comparing fixed-step and adaptive approaches before widespread library support — Surveying pre-2000s empirical studies and practitioner reports can provide evidence of whether fixed-step methods were preferred in resource-constrained environments, confirming the temporal qualifier of the hypothesis.

qualifier.temporal: prior to the availability of adaptive step-size control in standard libraries (pre-2000s)
qualifier.geographic: applicable to any computational environment with limited resources
